TS1 LFP Baseline

ibl-benchmark
lfp
ts1
decoding
First LFP-modality baseline for the ibl-benchmark TS1 suite: pipeline, bugs found, and the final 29-session results.
Author

Olivier Winter

Published

September 3, 2026

Overview

ibl-benchmark’s TS1 suite (behavior decoding from population activity) has no LFP-modality baseline. This analysis adds one: a classical band-power decoder, scored through the real bwb_eval submission pipeline on all 29 TS1 eval sessions, using lfpack-compressed LFP read straight off S3.

Code lives in ibl-benchmark at src/ts1/models/single_session/lfp/ (untracked at time of writing — not yet committed to the repo).

Method

Features: log Hilbert-amplitude envelope in four bands (delta 1-4 Hz, theta 4-8 Hz, beta 15-30 Hz, gamma 30-90 Hz), 96 channels per probe (4:1 spatial binning from 384), concatenated across a session’s probes. Read directly from /Users/olivier/Documents/datadisk/lfp-processing/lfpack/v03/lf_compressed_all.h5 (the “default” ~100x compression tier).

Trial windows, targets, splits: read directly off S3 via HTTP range requests against the official all_units eval build’s .h5 files — h5py supports any seekable file-like object, so opening the archive over HTTPS and only touching the small task_aligned_intervals / ts1_{split}_domain / ts1_normalize / behavior-branch groups (never spikes/units) keeps each session’s read to a few dozen small requests instead of a 0.6-4.4 GiB download. Verified byte-identical to the local-file path on a validation session before relying on it.

Decoders:

  • choice / reward / stimulus_contrast (sequence-level): mean-pooled window feature → StandardScaler → PCA(30) → LogisticRegressionCV.
  • wheel_speed / whisker_motion_energy / {left,right}_paw_speed / licking_rate (timestep-level): StandardScaler → PCA(120) → RidgeCV.

For both, training pools the causal train ∪ val domains (60% of the session) rather than just train (40%) — the sklearn estimators already do their own internal CV for hyperparameter selection, so a held-out validation split buys nothing extra. For the timestep tasks specifically, training uses the whole continuous train ∪ val trace (quiescent periods included), not just the ~300 disjoint 1 s trial windows — ~5x more samples, empirically the best of three training strategies tested (beat both trial-window-only and a movement-biased subset on every continuous task).

Test predictions are always restricted to the official per-trial windows, since that’s what bwb_eval ground truth covers.

wheel_speed and licking_rate predictions are clipped at 0 post-hoc: both are physically nonnegative and left unnormalized by the benchmark (wheel_speed = np.abs(velocity), licking_rate a count rate), so a negative prediction is never valid. whisker_motion_energy and the paw speeds are not clipped — those three are z-scored by the benchmark’s own ts1_normalize pipeline before scoring, so roughly half their legitimate values are negative by construction; clipping there would destroy real signal, not fix an error.

Bugs found and fixed along the way

  • Relative-vs-absolute timestamp bug: target timestamps returned by a trial’s own slice are relative to that trial’s start, but the LFP feature timestamps are absolute session-clock time. Interpolating one against the other directly means every query point lands hundreds to thousands of seconds outside the LFP’s finite domain — every continuous-task feature vector was silently corrupted by this until found. This alone was worth more than any later tuning: wheel_speed R² went from -0.053 to +0.023 on the session it was found on.
  • PCA(30) on ~85k pooled whole-domain samples was leaving real accuracy on the table purely as a regularization artifact: a components sweep (30/60/120/250/None x two alpha ranges) found PCA(120) consistently better on all three continuous tasks tested, e.g. wheel_speed 0.023 → 0.043 on the same session.
  • log1p on wheel_speed (tried on the hypothesis that a right-skewed, nonnegative target should fit better in log-space) made things worse, not better (0.043 → -0.019) — likely because log1p’s main benefit (compressing a long near-zero tail) doesn’t help where the model is actually scored: trial-locked windows where speed is already elevated, not near zero. Simple clipping at 0 was the better fix.

Discussion

Why is the continuous-task R² negative on average, when there’s clearly some signal? Pearson correlations are consistently positive (0.18-0.35) across wheel/paw/whisker, so this isn’t “no signal.” Two things are going on:

  1. TS1’s causal split evaluates on a genuinely held-out later block of the session, and restricts to already-moving trial windows. As a check, I reran the exact evaluation style of the earlier compression-benchmark scripts (2026-08-31_LFP_compression_decoding.py: whole continuous session, interleaved 5-fold non-shuffled CV, no movement-window restriction — not a valid TS1 score, purely diagnostic) on the same sessions and features: R² came back 0.10-0.26, matching or beating that script’s own 11-PID results (0.024-0.315, uncompressed). Same data, same decoder — the evaluation protocol alone explains most of the gap.
  2. Session-to-session heterogeneity is real and large: c958919c/8c025071/3bcb81b4 decode wheel speed well under the official protocol too (R² 0.11-0.15); f56194bc/ 6f6d2c8e are essentially unusable (R² -0.24 to -0.33). The 11 PIDs in the original compression benchmark were selected for a compression-fidelity demo, not sampled to represent the benchmark’s diversity, and none of them overlap with these 29 eval sessions.

whisker_motion_energy is the outlier: worst mean R² and by far the highest variance, and unlike the other three continuous tasks it also showed a real, sizeable bias (predicted mean off by more than half a z-scored std on the one session checked closely) that the PCA fix only partly addressed. Not root-caused.

Conclusion

LFP band power decodes reward and choice above chance from a simple linear pipeline, with reward the clearest win. The four continuous tasks show real but weak signal (positive correlation on most sessions) that a linear Ridge decoder can’t turn into positive R² under TS1’s causal-split, movement-window-only scoring on the majority of sessions — this looks like a genuine, still-open modeling problem rather than a pipeline bug, and whisker_motion_energy specifically has an unexplained bias worth a closer look.

Not yet done, worth doing before calling this submission-ready: wire this into a proper BaseModel/TS1EvalTrainer (the standalone-script shape doesn’t match the repo’s other baselines, e.g. CEBRA); run the benchmark’s 5 official EVAL_SEEDS instead of one; and the TS1 submission upload mechanics are themselves still marked TODO in ibl-benchmark’s own CONTRIBUTING.md, independent of anything here.

- **Relative-vs-absolute timestamp bug**: target timestamps returned by a trial's own slice
  are relative to that trial's `start`, but the LFP feature timestamps are absolute
  session-clock time. Interpolating one against the other directly means every query point

  feature vector was silently corrupted by this until found. This alone was worth more than

- **PCA(30) on ~85k pooled whole-domain samples** was leaving real accuracy on the table

  ranges) found PCA(120) consistently better on all three continuous tasks tested, e.g.

- **log1p on wheel_speed** (tried on the hypothesis that a right-skewed, nonnegative target
  should fit better in log-space) made things *worse*, not better (0.043 → -0.019) — likely

**Why is the continuous-task R² negative on average, when there's clearly some signal?**

unlike the other three continuous tasks it also showed a real, sizeable bias (predicted mean
off by more than half a z-scored std on the one session checked closely) that the PCA fix
